rv.q: Love as a battlefield on which nobody wins has seldom been mapped as thrillingly as it is in Daniel Aukin’s definitive revival of this bruising drama from 1983.

What's missing is the claustrophobic intensity that made the original production so memorable. Instead of feeling trapped in a seedy motel room with these desperate characters, you're watching them from a comfortable distance.
Until its brilliant final 15 minutes, Aukin’s production doesn’t have that magnetic force.
But it’s Rockwell and Arianda who really strike the sparks, blow on the embers and get the fire raging.
Rockwell's performance never lets us forget that "Fool for Love" is a dark and twisted comedy.
But the heat only occasionally rises above a simmer, and despite all the tequila being gulped onstage, the whole thing feels a tad too correct in Manhattan Theatre Club’s bijou Broadway house.
Actors love this play, as do student audiences.

When the withholding and revelation are handled as adroitly as they are in Daniel Aukin's terrific staging for the Manhattan Theatre Club, Fool for Love acquires the force of Greek tragedy — one Greek tragedy in particular.

Although Arianda and Rockwell have the looks, the presence and the guts, there isn't the down-and-dirty chemistry that makes the fate of the lovers' long and conflicted relationship feel inevitable and dangerous.
The bonds of blood and lust are deep, Fool for Love reminds us, and not even this tough-talking cowboy can shrug them off.
It’s all handled with an enormous amount of skill and affection -- the 75 minutes fly by, and we feel as if we know these folks intimately.
Here, though, Rockwell and Arianda gleefully tear into one another, generating palpable sexual tension and nailing the grimly comic underbelly of Shepard's dialogue.
Arianda, ever fascinating, turns on a dime from light to dark.
Amid all that sound and fury, there is not much in this play that resonates beyond some stylish writing and a chance for a quartet of fine actors to strut their stuff.
But with this worthy company gone and any Shepard play always an event, his fans won't want to miss this starry revival.
From Eddie's first words: 'I'm not leaving,' you are in the play's intense grip
It's the most potent concentration of theatrical mind games we're likely to see on Broadway for a long time.
Still, there's great pleasure in seeing these two masters duking it out over a card table.
Daniel Aukin's focused, highly physical revival is built around the intense interplay between Arianda and Rockwell.
If you’re a theatergoer who loves commanding performances focusing on complex characters, this is your play.

In the revival, in a much larger theater that perhaps diminishes the flow of the characters’ feelings, the visceral energy – and sexual tension — is much lower, allowing us to notice how modest the play really is.
However, amid all that sound and fury, there is not much in this play that resonates beyond some stylish writing and a chance for a quartet of fine actors to strut their stuff.
“Fool for Love” struck me as little more than an impressive acting exercise and the theatrical equivalent of a low-budget action flick.
Fools for realism, these lovers never make it outside the motel room and into the vast night beyond.
At its heart, this production is irredeemably nice, perhaps the most devastating quality for any Fool for Love.
Couples arguing is a fixture of the American stage, but these two are just human bumper cars.
With this phenomenal production, Fool For Love rightfully takes its place as one of the most important American plays of its generation.
Fool for Love is a bright example of Sam Shepard at his best, and if you’re not familiar with his work, this production is a ‘must-see.’
Together they are electric and this play for 75 minutes burn as bright as the lights on Broadway.
The insights that Shepard brings in regards to our relationships with those who we love, and specially those who are wrong for us, are nothing short of brilliant.
In their hands, this looks to be Shepard's masterpiece, his work most likely to stand the test of time.

Aukin’s slightly revisionist but extraordinarily meticulous direction, Sam Rockwell and Nina Arianda capture the angst and desperation of their characters and bring their struggle to separate and individuate to a cathartic frenzy that make a deep and lasting impression on the audience...'Fool for Love' is a must see.
A show chock-full of jaw-on-your-floor moments.
With energy and talent bouncing off the walls of the Friedman Theatre, Manhattan Theatre Club delivers a doozy of a production of this stellar work.
While this show might be too raw for many tourists, I found the acting and play riveting.
Rockwell brings layers of pain and anger and vulnerability to a role that could easily be paper thin in less capable hands.
These two inexorably entwined lovers are doomed to repeat their patterns over and over.

Not only is physical intimacy sacrificed but the larger stage seems to highlight its relative lack of plot development; its overdependence on long narrative monologues sometimes make it seem more an advanced acting exercise than a fully articulated drama.
Manhattan Theater Club’s production is simmering and sultry thanks to this fine cast whose only addiction is a commitment to quality acting.

Eddie, a well chosen Rockwell, is a lasso-circling, bow-legged, beaten down cowboy, who thoroughly understands and connects to all the deeper emotional turmoil as if he actually experienced every moment of the character.
While the play lurches a little towards the end, Shepard weaves compellingly sad poetry out of the wasted lives of his characters, which this production makes real and vivid.
Here, in Daniel Aukin’s somewhat misguided production (first done two years ago at the Williamstown Theatre Festival), we’re merely watching them from a safe distance.
As an acting exercise, you can’t improve on the casting of Sam Rockwell and Nina Arianda as Eddie and May respectively.
I wish I had found it more involving.
Fool for Love’s tantalizing passion is captured in this alluring image and that quality is woefully absent in this adequate and lackluster revival.
I found it dreadfully mediocre, and even boring despite its mere 75-minute running time
